cim: DOJ’s New Super Intelligence Task Force Signals More Coordinated AI Enforcement
cim_eredeti: DOJ’s New Super Intelligence Task Force Signals More Coordinated AI Enforcement
szoveg_eredeti:
In September 2026, President Trump issued Executive Order 14434, “Inaugurating the Era of Super Intelligence,” requiring the executive branch to use the term “Super Intelligence” in place of “Artificial Intelligence” to the “maximum extent permitted by law.”[1] On Nov. 5, the DOJ announced the formation of the DOJ-SITF, an SI task force led by Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward and Associate Deputy Attorney General Stephen Weiss.[2]

According to the DOJ, the DOJ-SITF “will ensure that America’s leadership in SI is not compromised by the misuse of SI by foreign state and state-sponsored actors, transnational criminal organizations, and individual or corporate actors engaged in fraud or other unlawful conduct.”[3] This mandate therefore extends beyond foreign and transnational threats to domestic individuals and companies whose use of advanced AI implicates fraud or other unlawful conduct.

The Nov. 5 announcement followed an Oct. 13 internal DOJ memorandum establishing the DOJ-SITF (the SITF Memo).[4] According to the SITF Memo, the Task Force will have a comprehensive approach to SI that includes:

The SITF Memo also contemplates increased visibility by the DOJ-SITF into SI-related matters being handled elsewhere in the DOJ. At the Task Force’s request, the DOJ components and U.S. Attorneys’ Offices may be required to provide notice when seeking to open an investigation involving SI, before seeking charges and before finalizing a resolution.[6] The DOJ-SITF plans to develop a notification process, although the memo provides that notification should not “delay action” or “be necessary in exigent circumstances, including imminent threats to public safety or risk of loss of evidence.”[7]

The DOJ-SITF represents a significant centralization of the DOJ’s approach to AI-related matters. The DOJ’s previous Artificial Intelligence Litigation Task Force[8] primarily focused on challenging state-level AI laws deemed inconsistent with the administration’s goal of advancing a “minimally burdensome national policy framework for AI.”[9] Although the DOJ-SITF will continue that work, it has a materially broader mandate encompassing criminal and civil enforcement, public safety, compliance guidance, and coordination of SI-related matters across the DOJ.

Companies should expect AI-related matters within the DOJ to become more coordinated, and potentially more consistent, across components and U.S. Attorneys’ Offices. The DOJ-SITF is charged with organizing enforcement efforts, deconflicting matters, identifying enforcement priorities and developing guidance concerning unlawful SI-related conduct. Its contemplated notification process also may give the Task Force visibility into matters at significant stages of an investigation, including opening, charging and resolution.

The compliance component deserves particular attention. The DOJ-SITF is expressly charged with developing guidance concerning the “evaluation of compliance measures,” and DOJ’s public announcement identified regular reporting of SI risks and incidents and “vigorous internal controls” as areas of focus. Companies developing or deploying advanced AI should therefore consider whether their governance structures identify responsibility for AI-related risk, establish escalation and incident-reporting mechanisms, and document significant decisions involving advanced AI systems.

The DOJ-SITF also, through the Offices of Legal Policy and Legislative Affairs, plans to advise on legislative and regulatory proposals that promote SI innovation “without burdensome regulation.”[10] This function may become particularly significant as the 120th Congress considers its own approach to AI regulation. The administration and incoming Congress may not share the same views on the appropriate balance between innovation, safety, accountability and federal regulation. DOJ-SITF may therefore operate not only as an enforcement-coordination body but also as an important executive branch voice in the developing federal AI policy debate.

The DOJ-SITF is the latest sign that the federal government’s approach to AI is evolving alongside the technology itself. For companies, the most immediate significance may be greater coordination of AI-related matters across the DOJ and increased attention to the adequacy of corporate compliance measures. Organizations developing or deploying advanced AI should monitor the Task Force’s emerging enforcement priorities and guidance and consider whether their existing governance, escalation, incident-response and documentation practices would withstand DOJ scrutiny.

[1] Exec. Order No. 14,434, 91 Fed. Reg. 63129 (Sept. 29, 2026).

[2] Press Release, Dep’t of Just., Department of Justice Launches Super Intelligence Task Force (Nov. 5, 2026), available at https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/department-justice-launches-super-intelligence-task-force.

[4] Memorandum from the Office of the Attorney General, Super Intelligence Task Force, Dep’t of Just. (Oct. 13, 2026), available at https://www.justice.gov/opa/media/1470291/dl?inline.

[8] For more, see our previous alert, Navigating the Emerging Federal-State AI Showdown: DOJ Establishes AI Litigation Task Force (Jan. 20, 2026), available at https://www.bakerlaw.com/insights/navigating-the-emerging-federal-state-ai-showdown-doj-establishes-ai-litigation-task-force/.

[9] Exec. Order No. 14,365, 90 Fed. Reg. 58499 (Dec. 16, 2025).
